summary: This Wikipedia-derived note surveys Nanjing, a major Yangtze River city in eastern China, covering its long history as a capital of many dynasties and regimes, its economy and population statistics, its transport and Yangtze bridges, museums, education, sports, culture and tourism. It also recounts traumatic episodes such as the Taiping-era slaughter of 1864 and the Nanjing Massacre. The text is a broad overview rather than a focused account of any single period.
one_line: Overview of Nanjing, the historic Yangtze River capital of Jiangsu covering its dynastic history, economy, population, bridges, museums and culture.
key_facts: Nanjing is the capital city of Jiangsu province and the second largest city in East China, with a total population of 8,216,100.
Nanjing served as the capital of Eastern Wu, the Eastern Jin and each of the Southern Dynasties, and the Ming dynasty when all of China was ruled from the city (1368-1421).
The name Nanjing means "Southern Capital", and the city is particularly known as Jinling (金陵, literally Gold Mountain).
In 2013 the city's GDP was RMB 801 billion (3rd in Jiangsu), and GDP per capita was RMB 98,174 (US$16041).
The Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge, the first, was begun in 1960 and opened to traffic in 1968, spanning 4,600 metres on the upper deck.
The census population of the City of Nanjing reached 8.005 million in 2010, and was estimated at 8.11 million in 2011.
When Qing forces led by Zeng Guofan retook the city in 1864, over 100,000 were estimated to have committed suicide or fought to the death.
The Yangtze River was crossed by five bridges and two tunnels as of October 2014.
Nanjing Museum, formerly the National Central Museum during the ROC period, is the first modern museum in China and has 400,000 items in its permanent collection.
The annual International Plum Blossom Festival is held in Plum Blossom Hill, the largest plum collection in China.
Nanjing was the seat of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (1851-64) and the Japanese puppet regime of Wang Jingwei (1940-45).
In 1999, 77,394 residents belonged to minority nationalities, of whom 64,832 were Hui; Han made up 98.56 percent of the population.
Nanjing is one of the fifteen sub-provincial cities in the People's Republic of China's administrative structure.
Nanjing's Yangyshan Quarry holds a gigantic stele, cut on the orders of the Yongle Emperor, abandoned about 600 years ago.
